title: Is philosophy supposed to change things?
teaches: Alienation, and Marx's diagnosis set apart from his failed predictions

blocks.text: On 17 March 1883, about a dozen people stood at a grave in Highgate Cemetery in north London. They were burying a German exile who had lived in London for more than 30 years, mostly in poverty, writing in the Reading Room of the British Museum. His closest friend[^engels-mill] gave a short speech saying that his name and his work would endure through the ages. Few newspapers in Britain noticed the death.

Within 70 years, about a third of the world's population lived under governments that called themselves Marxist. Karl Marx's grave now has a large bronze head on a granite base, put up in 1956, and on the base is a sentence he wrote in a notebook in 1845, at the age of 26: "The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point, however, is to change it."[^theses]

blocks.caption: Karl Marx photographed by John Mayall in London in 1875.

blocks.text: People often run together two distinct parts of Marx's work: his diagnosis of what is wrong with work under capitalism, much of which is still taken seriously, and his predictions about what would happen next, most of which did not come true.

In 1844, living in Paris, Marx filled notebooks with thoughts on economics and philosophy. They were not published until 1932, and their central idea, **alienation**, became one of his most influential. Marx thought human beings are by nature makers: we express ourselves and realise our abilities by working on the world, making things, alone and with others. Under capitalism most people work for wages, making things they do not own, by methods they do not choose, for the profit of someone else.

Marx described four ways the worker is cut off, or alienated. From the product, which belongs to the employer and confronts the worker as something alien. From the activity of work itself, which is forced and not a free expression of who they are. From their own human nature as makers. And from other people, who become competitors or bosses. "The worker therefore only feels himself outside his work, and in his work feels outside himself. He is at home when he is not working, and when he is working he is not at home."

Marx imagined a society, after capitalism, where this would end. In a well-known passage he and Engels wrote that there it would be possible "to hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon, rear cattle in the evening, criticise after dinner", without ever becoming a hunter, fisherman, herdsman or critic. He never described in any detail how such a society would work.

options.ask: Is most paid work in a modern economy alienating, in Marx's sense: done for someone else, in ways you do not choose, and not an expression of who you are?
choices: Yes, for most people
For many people, but not most
No: most people find real meaning in their work
Not sure
who: You chose Marx's answer. Surveys of job satisfaction give mixed support: many people say they are satisfied, and many say their work is not meaningful.
You chose the answer many sociologists of work give: it depends heavily on the job and the control people have over it.
You chose the answer Marx's critics give. Marx would ask whether people would still do the work if they did not need the wage.
The evidence is mixed, so many researchers are unsure too.

blocks.text: Marx's larger theory was about history. With his friend Friedrich Engels he argued that what shapes a society most is how it produces what it needs: its tools, its technology, and who owns them. Laws, politics, religion and philosophy grow up to fit that economic base and to protect the people who own it. "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles", begins *The Communist Manifesto* (1848).

This made Marx, with Nietzsche in lesson 18 and later Freud, one of what the philosopher Paul Ricoeur called the "masters of suspicion": thinkers who taught people to ask what interests lie hidden behind ideas that claim to be about truth or morality. Nietzsche suspected that morality expressed the resentment of the weak. Marx suspected that the ideas of each age expressed the interests of its ruling class. "The ruling ideas of each age have ever been the ideas of its ruling class." Religion, he wrote, was "the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, and the soul of soulless conditions. It is the opium of the people." The famous last sentence is usually quoted without the sympathy that comes before it.

Marx predicted that capitalism would collapse from its own contradictions. Competition would drive wages down to the minimum needed to survive, the *Manifesto* of 1848 said. Wealth would gather in fewer and fewer hands, and crises would get worse. Eventually the workers of the most industrial countries, such as Britain and Germany, would rise up and take the means of production into common ownership, and the state itself would, in Engels's phrase, "wither away". Some of his analysis has held up well; much of the prediction did not.

blocks.caption: Eight claims from Marx's writings. Sort each by how it has fared since.

items.name: Capitalism spreads across the globe, seeking new markets everywhere
items.why: The Manifesto's description of globalisation reads as if written much later.

items.name: Capitalist economies go through repeated booms and crises
items.why: Economists of many schools agree that market economies have recurring crises.

items.name: Work done for others, with no control, can leave people cut off from it
items.why: Alienation is still studied in sociology and psychology of work.

items.name: Economic interests shape laws, politics and ideas
items.why: Few historians think they explain everything; most think they explain a great deal.

items.name: Wages will fall to the bare minimum needed to survive
items.why: Real wages in industrial countries rose many times over in the century after Marx.

items.name: Revolution will come first in the most industrial countries
items.why: The first Marxist revolution came in Russia in 1917, then mostly peasant farmers.

items.name: After the revolution, the state will wither away
items.why: Engels's phrase. The states built in Marx's name became some of the most powerful and repressive in history.

items.name: Society will split into two great classes, owners and workers
items.why: A large middle class of salaried and professional workers grew instead.

blocks.text: The governments that called themselves Marxist in the 20th century, in the Soviet Union, China, Cambodia and elsewhere, were responsible for famines, purges and labour camps in which tens of millions died. Whether this followed from Marx's ideas or betrayed them is one of the most argued-over questions in modern history. Marx said little about how a society after capitalism would be run or how power in it would be checked, and critics argue that this silence left the way open to dictatorship.

blocks.caption: The sentence on Marx's tomb. Your answer is saved on the Verdicts page.

options.ask: Is the job of philosophy to understand the world, or to change it?
choices: To understand it: change should be left to citizens and politicians
To change it: understanding that changes nothing is idle
Understanding comes first, and good change depends on it
Not sure
who: You chose a view common among academic philosophers today.
You chose the answer of many who admire Marx's analysis and fear what was done in his name.
Socrates, in lesson 1, would say examining the question is already a kind of change.

blocks.text: Marx's predictions of revolution and the withering of the state have been abandoned, even by most scholars who call themselves Marxists. His diagnosis is still argued over: alienation in the sociology of work, the influence of economic interests on ideas in history and political philosophy, and capitalism's tendency to crisis and inequality in economics, especially since the financial crisis of 2008. A school called analytical Marxism, led by the philosopher G. A. Cohen from the 1970s, restated his ideas with the tools of analytic philosophy and dropped those that failed. *Capital* is still one of the most cited books in the social sciences.[^capital]

blocks.caption: Four questions on Marx
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What did Marx mean by alienation?
choices: Workers are cut off from what they make, from their work, from their human nature as makers, and from each other
Workers move to cities and lose touch with their families
People from other countries feel out of place in a new society
Intellectuals feel cut off from ordinary people
items.why: "He is at home when he is not working, and when he is working he is not at home."

items.ask: Why did Paul Ricoeur call Marx, Nietzsche and Freud masters of suspicion?
choices: They taught people to look for hidden interests or drives behind ideas that claim to be about truth or morality
They were all suspected of crimes by the police
They all distrusted science
They all wrote in secret codes
items.why: For Marx, the ruling ideas of each age are the ideas of its ruling class.

items.ask: Which of Marx's predictions did NOT happen?
choices: Revolution would come first in the most industrial countries
Capitalism would spread across the globe
Market economies would have repeated crises
Economic interests would shape politics
items.why: The first Marxist revolution was in Russia, a mostly peasant country.

items.ask: What did Marx say religion was, in the passage that ends "the opium of the people"?
choices: The sigh of the oppressed creature and the heart of a heartless world
A plot by priests to keep workers poor
A harmless pastime with no effect on society
The highest expression of human reason
items.why: The sympathy before the last line is usually left out.

summary: **Philosophy should change the world.** Marx wrote in 1845 that philosophers had only interpreted the world, and that the point is to change it.
**Wage work alienates people from themselves.** Workers are cut off from their product, their work, their nature and each other, and feel at home only when not working.
**Ownership of production shapes history.** Ideas tend to serve the ruling class, so Marx, a master of suspicion with Nietzsche and Freud, looked for interests hidden behind them.
**Marx's diagnosis outlasted his predictions.** Wages rose, the revolution came in Russia, and the state did not wither.

theses.title: The Theses on Feuerbach
theses.text: The sentence is the eleventh of eleven short notes Marx wrote in 1845 about the philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach. Engels found them after Marx's death and published them in 1888, with small changes; the tomb uses Engels's version.

capital.title: Capital
capital.text: Marx published the first volume of Capital in 1867. It sold slowly; the first edition of 1,000 copies took four years to sell out. Engels assembled volumes two and three from Marx's drafts after his death.

engels-mill.title: Engels and the cotton mill
engels-mill.text: Marx's closest friend was Friedrich Engels, the son of a wealthy German textile manufacturer. For nearly twenty years Engels worked in the family's cotton mill in Manchester, using his income to support Marx and his family in London.
